title-group.article-title: Glofitamab monotherapy in patients with Richter transformation: safety and efficacy from a phase 1 study

body.p: Richter transformation (RT) is characterized by the transformation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).1,2 The incidence of DLBCL-type RT is ∼0.5% to 1% per year after CLL diagnosis, with an overall prevalence of 2% to 10%.1,3 Patients with RT have a poor prognosis, with an estimated median overall survival (OS) of 8 to 12 months.1,2,4 RT often develops in patients undergoing active CLL treatment, and targeted monotherapies such as Bruton tyrosine kinase and B-cell lymphoma-2 inhibitors demonstrate limited activity in RT.4 RT is rarely curable, and standard chemotherapy results in lower response rates and shorter durations of response vs other DLBCL subtypes.1,4,5 With no current standard of care,1,2,4 there remains an unmet medical need for novel efficacious therapies for RT.

Glofitamab, a CD20×CD3 T-cell engaging bispecific antibody, redirects T cells to eliminate B cells.6 Glofitamab is an off-the-shelf, fixed-duration therapy administered across twelve 21-day cycles. Obinutuzumab pretreatment (1000 mg) mitigates cytokine release syndrome (CRS) risk through the initial depletion of B cells.6, 7, 8

NP30179 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03075696) is an ongoing 3-part phase 1/2 multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation/dose-expansion study of glofitamab monotherapy. Previously, fixed-duration glofitamab monotherapy demonstrated durable responses and a manageable safety profile in relapsed/refractory DLBCL.7 Based on these results, glofitamab was approved for patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines of therapy.9,10 We present the preliminary safety and efficacy of glofitamab monotherapy in patients with RT from the NP30179 study.

This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, Good Clinical Practice guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation, and applicable laws. An internal monitoring committee reviewed safety and efficacy data and made study conduct recommendations. All patients provided written informed consent.

Patients aged ≥18 years with ≥1 prior systemic therapy, including ≥1 anti-CD20 antibody, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 to 1 were included. Patients with CLL only, Burkitt lymphoma, and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma were excluded. Full eligibility criteria have previously been described.7

Obinutuzumab (1000 mg) was administered 7 days before the first glofitamab dose (1 patient received 2000 mg). IV glofitamab monotherapy was administered at a fixed dose (0.6, 1.0, 1.8, 10, or 25 mg) or with step-up dosing (SUD) in cycle 1 (day 8, 2.5 mg; day 15, 10 mg), up to a target dose of 16 or 30 mg on cycle 2 day 1, either every 2 or every 3 weeks for ≤12 cycles (supplemental Table 1). Efficacy was investigator assessed using Lugano criteria11; end points for the RT subgroup included investigator-assessed complete response (CR) rate, overall response rate (ORR), duration of CR (DoCR), time to first CR, progression-free survival (PFS), and OS. Adverse events (AEs) were graded per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) (version 4.03); CRS was graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) criteria 2019.12 Details are provided in the supplemental Appendix; full methods have previously been described.7

As of 8 September 2025, a total of 11 patients with RT had received glofitamab at either a fixed dose (0.6-25 mg, n = 5) or with SUD (2.5/10/16 mg, n = 3; 2.5/10/30 mg, n = 3). The median age was 71 years (range, 48-77), 63.6% had bulky disease (>6 cm), 90.9% had Ann Arbor stage III/IV disease, and 45.5% had an International Prognostic Index score of ≥3 (supplemental Table 2). Data for clonal relatedness were not available. The median number of prior therapies for CLL/RT was 3 (range, 1-4); 54.5% of the patients had received ≥3 prior therapies. All patients received prior rituximab-chemotherapy to treat their RT; no patients received glofitamab as their first RT treatment. Most patients were refractory to a prior anti-CD20 antibody-containing regimen (90.9%) and all to their most recent regimen.

A high number of responses were observed with glofitamab monotherapy; 7 of the 11 patients achieved an investigator-assessed response (partial response or CR), including 5 patients with a best response of CR. The median time to response (partial response/CR) was 1.4 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2-2.5); the median time to CR was 2.5 months (95% CI, 1.4 to not estimable [NE]). The activity observed with glofitamab monotherapy is within the same range as the ORR and CR rates seen with other investigational therapies in RT, such as tislelizumab-zanubrutinib (n = 48; 58% and 19%, respectively),13 venetoclax plus dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (n = 20; 80% and 65%, respectively),14 pirtobrutinib (n = 82; 50% and 13%, respectively),15 mosunetuzumab (n = 20; 40% and 20%, respectively),16 and epcoritamab (n = 26; 50% and 35%, respectively).17 Most patients achieved ≥50% reduction in tumor size (supplemental Figure 1).

Six patients progressed during treatment, all within the first 9 months of the study. Among patients who achieved CR, the median follow-up was 67.1 months (95% CI, 55.5 to NE). Most of these patients (4/5 [80.0%]) remained in remission at data cutoff, and those with longer follow-up were in remission for ∼80 months after treatment ended. The median DoCR was NE (95% CI, 5.5 to NE). One patient had a DoCR lasting ∼6 months before progression; for the remaining patients with CR, the DoCR ranged from 55 to 74 months at the clinical cutoff date (Figure 1). None of these patients received consolidation treatment after completing glofitamab therapy. After a median time on glofitamab of 5.5 months (range, 0.5-7.6), the median PFS and OS were 3.5 months (95% CI, 1.8 to NE; median follow-up, 69.6 months) and NE (95% CI, 3.4 to NE; median follow-up, 66.5 months), respectively.Figure 1.

All patients reported an AE, with 7 (63.6%) reporting a grade 3/4 AE (Table 1). No grade 5 AEs were reported. The most common (≥10% of patients) grade 3/4 AEs were neutropenia (27.3%), thrombocytopenia (18.2%), and CRS (18.2%). Serious AEs were reported in 72.7% of the patients, with 54.5% deemed related to glofitamab. No AEs led to discontinuation of glofitamab/obinutuzumab, and 2 (18.2%) led to glofitamab dose modification/interruption.Table 1.

CRS was the most common AE (n = 8 [72.7%]); 3 patients received tocilizumab plus corticosteroids, and 1 patient received tocilizumab alone for CRS management. CRS was mostly low grade (grade 1, 27.3%; grade 2, 27.3%; grade 3, 9.1%; grade 4, 9.1%) and occurred during cycles 1 to 2 with SUD (supplemental Figure 2). This is consistent with observations of other bispecific antibodies in RT, such as epcoritamab (any-grade CRS, 90%; grade 1, 40%; grade 2, 50%)18 and mosunetuzumab (any-grade CRS, 65%; grade 1, 20%; grade 2, 40%).16 The CRS rates should be interpreted with caution, considering the small sample size and potential for further optimization of CRS management in patients with RT. Other AEs of interest (all grades) included infections/infestations (54.5%), neutropenia (45.5%), AEs potentially consistent with immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (syncope and confusional state; 9.1% each), and tumor flare (9.1%; supplemental Table 3).

Limitations of this study include the small sample size, the use of different dosing regimens, and the potential underestimation of the drug’s activity/toxicity as most patients were treated below the established dose for DLBCL (2.5/10/30 mg). Further research is needed in this population; phase 2 studies of glofitamab monotherapy or in combination with other agents in RT are ongoing (ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT06043674 and NCT06186648).

In conclusion, fixed-duration glofitamab monotherapy demonstrated promising activity in heavily pretreated and highly refractory patients with RT. With a long follow-up (67.1 months), durable and ongoing CRs were observed. The safety profile of glofitamab was characterized by mostly low-grade CRS, with no AEs leading to treatment withdrawal at the doses evaluated. Glofitamab represents a potential therapy for patients with RT who have a high unmet need.
